articles.title: From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa
articles.summary: October 27 vote could test whether Israel’s ties with African countries withstand the fallout from the war on Gaza.
articles.body:
Lagos, Nigeria – As Israelis prepare to vote on October 27, African governments from Pretoria to Rabat are weighing what the result could mean for their own foreign and domestic policies.

The war on Gaza has exposed sharp differences across the continent, with some governments pursuing diplomatic measures against Israel while others maintain commercial and security ties.

Recent polling has shown a closely contested race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads and a bloc of Jewish-led opposition parties .

Neither is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with a protracted period of coalition talks expected to follow the vote.

The next government’s approach to Gaza and the Palestinian question could influence Israel’s efforts to preserve and expand its partnerships across the continent.

Israel’s relationships across Africa are shaped by competing priorities. While the Gaza war has intensified diplomatic pressure and public opposition in many countries, security needs, commercial interests and longstanding bilateral partnerships continue to influence government decisions.

Since the war began in October 2023, South Africa has emerged as one of Israel’s most vocal critics in Africa. Its government brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention. Israel rejects the allegations. The court’s so-called provisional measures in 2024, including an order for Israel to take action to prevent acts of genocide, are not a final ruling on whether genocide has occurred.

In November 2023, South Africa’s National Assembly adopted a motion calling on the government to close the Israeli embassy and suspend diplomatic relations. The motion did not itself implement those measures, but it underscored the strength of political opposition to Israel’s military campaign.

Other African governments have taken different approaches that reflect national political priorities and foreign policy calculations rather than a single continental position.

Chad recalled its ambassador to Israel in November 2023, while some countries have maintained relations despite criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Morocco offers a contrasting example. It restored relations with Israel in 2020 under a US-backed arrangement linked to Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Despite public demonstrations opposing normalisation, Rabat has continued to pursue closer ties.

On September 16, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita met in New York at a trilateral summit hosted by US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz. The three countries reaffirmed plans to upgrade diplomatic relations, elevate their respective missions to embassies and appoint ambassadors.

They also agreed to conclude investment protection and double taxation agreements by the end of this year, expand flights to include Moroccan airlines and arrange reciprocal high-level visits in the coming months. These were announced commitments, rather than confirmation that the changes had already been implemented.

For Idowu Johnson, associate professor of international relations at the University of Ibadan, the diversity of African states makes it difficult to predict a uniform response to Israel’s election.

“Africa’s heterogeneity means individual states have handled relations with Israel separately. Since the October 7, 2023 attacks, African criticism has focused on Israel’s denial of Palestinian statehood.

“The October 27 election will therefore be pivotal, as a new government’s stance on the Palestinian cause will shape how far Africa cooperates on agriculture, trade, security and technology, guided by self-determination and international law as well as bilateral interests,” Johnson said.

Israel’s relationship with the African Union (AU) also reflects these divisions. In 2021, the AU Commission chairperson accredited Israel’s representative to the organisation, prompting objections from member states.

In February 2022, the AU Assembly established a committee of heads of state and government to consult on Israel’s observer status. The dispute continued into 2023, when the AU moved to suspend Israel’s accreditation pending further consideration.

The disagreement has reflected wider divisions over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and the organisation’s approach to the conflict.

A new Israeli government could seek to ease those tensions, but any change would depend on its policies as well as the positions of AU member states.

Security ties may outlast diplomatic tensions

Security cooperation has been a significant part of Israel’s relationships with some African governments. Israeli companies have pursued defence and security contracts involving equipment, surveillance technology and training.

But the nature and scale of those relationships vary by country and claims about particular agreements or technologies should be tied to documented cases rather than treated as evidence of a uniform Israeli security presence across the continent.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo offers a recent example of efforts to deepen cooperation. Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi visited Israel on August 31 and September 1, meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog. Discussions covered security, defence, agriculture, infrastructure, energy and high technology. Both sides expressed a desire to strengthen their strategic partnership and expand cooperation across several sectors.

The visit followed memorandums of understanding signed on July 27. Congolese officials said the visit would review those agreements and explore further Israeli investment, including opportunities linked to the Lobito Corridor. The meetings demonstrate the potential scope of bilateral cooperation, but do not establish that a specific new security contract has been concluded.

For governments confronting armed groups, insecurity can create incentives to seek equipment, intelligence and training from foreign partners. Yet the importance of Israeli cooperation differs between countries and diplomatic tensions will not necessarily have the same effect on every security relationship.

The limits of Israel’s diplomatic outreach were also evident after it recognised Somaliland as an independent state on December 26, last year, the first country to do so. Somalia and other critics rejected the move, arguing that it undermined Somalia’s territorial integrity. The decision triggered demonstrations in Somalia and Somaliland.

Speaking to Al Jazeera this month, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said Somalia will not accept Israeli presence in the country “under any circumstances”. He added that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, adding that its real aim was to get closer to the Gulf states and Iran.

According to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project (ACLED), 110 demonstrations directly linked to Israel’s Somaliland recognition had been recorded by the time of its February 2026 Africa overview. Only seven supported the move, all in Somaliland; the others opposed it. The figures cover demonstrations linked to that particular decision, not all African views of Israel, and should not be treated as a continent-wide measure of public opinion.

Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an Africa analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute, argues that public opposition can constrain governments even when they see strategic value in maintaining ties.

“The strongest constraint, however, may come from African publics rather than governments: the Somaliland recognition drew widespread opposition, the African Union and many governments reaffirmed Somalia’s territorial integrity, and ACLED logged 110 related demonstrations, only seven in support.

“Depending on its approach, the next Israeli government could therefore either deepen strategic cooperation in Morocco, Sudan and the Red Sea, or face a legitimacy problem if it continues policies seen as tied to the Gaza war, widening the gap between state-level cooperation and public sentiment,” Ibrahim told Al Jazeera.

The Somaliland episode shows how a diplomatic move can provoke opposition when it is perceived to challenge a core principle of sovereignty.

It does not, by itself, establish that African governments will abandon security agreements with Israel. The consequences will depend on the countries involved, the terms of their cooperation and the domestic political costs of maintaining them.

Trade, agritech and the contest for influence

Trade and development cooperation offer Israel another route to maintaining relationships in Africa. Israeli firms and officials have pursued partnerships in areas including agriculture, irrigation, water management, health and technology.

Such cooperation can offer practical benefits to governments seeking investment and technical expertise, but commercial ties do not necessarily translate into public support for Israel’s policies.

Zambia illustrates Israel’s efforts to deepen bilateral engagement. Israel opened a resident embassy in Lusaka in August last year, after a 52-year absence. Agriculture, water management, health, education and technology have been identified as potential areas for closer cooperation. The move formed part of Israel’s broader effort to strengthen its engagement with African countries.

Some analysts have interpreted Israel’s renewed engagement with Zambia as an attempt to cultivate partners who could counterbalance South Africa’s influence in the region. That remains an interpretation, not an established explanation for the relationship.

Zambia has its own reasons for seeking investment and cooperation, particularly in agriculture, water management and technology; closer bilateral ties alone do not prove that countering South Africa is Israel’s objective.

Professor Iwebunor Okwechime, of Obafemi Awolowo University, points to the historical roots of South Africa’s position towards Israel.

“If we trace the stance South Africa took, it goes back to the apartheid era, when Israel backed the apartheid regime and refused to support the struggle against the minority government. This historical context is important for understanding South Africa-Israel relations today,” Okwechime told Al Jazeera.

For African governments, the challenge will be to balance security and commercial interests against public opposition, commitments to Palestinian rights and positions on international law. For Israel, the upcoming election will test whether a new government can ease diplomatic tensions across Africa without fundamentally changing the policies that have fuelled them.

As Okwechime told Al Jazeera, “There won’t be a radical change in sentiments regardless of the government in power”.

articles.title: Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
articles.summary: Timekeepers add a leap second occasionally to keep our clocks and the Earth’s rotation in tune. That could now change.
articles.body:
The world’s timekeepers are meeting on Thursday near Paris to decide whether to scrap the “leap second”, which could disconnect the clocks we use from the Earth’s rotation and realign timescales.

The world’s clocks are designed on the idea that the Earth completes one rotation on its axis in exactly 24 hours. But it actually wobbles, making the time the Earth takes to rotate less exact. And over time, the Earth’s rotation is gradually slowing.

To compensate for that, since 1972, timekeepers have added a leap second every few years – the last one was added in 2016 – to keep clocks and Earth’s rotation in synchronisation.

But pressure has been mounting to scrap the leap second since it complicates matters for financial markets and data centres, which rely on precise timing down to milliseconds.

So what is a leap second? Could it be scrapped? And how might it change our understanding of time?

Clocks work based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the global standard that has been based on high-precision atomic clocks for more than seven decades. Atomic clocks mark time by observing the vibration of atoms.

But the Earth’s rotation works independently of atomic clocks.

A leap second is a second added periodically to UTC to make it synchronise with the Earth’s rotation. The first leap second was added to world clocks in 1972.

There have been 27 leap seconds added so far with the previous leap second being added on December 31, 2016. No further leap seconds have been added since.

According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), a nonregulatory federal agency of the United States Department of Commerce, leap seconds occur at the end of December or the end of June. The NIST also cites differences between the precision of the atomic second and the Earth’s rotation to explain the need for a leap second.

“The speed of the Earth’s rotation is not constant. …. This gradual decrease in the rotational rate is causing the duration of the mean solar second to gradually increase with respect to the atomic second,” the NIST added.

Why is pressure mounting to scrap leap seconds?

While leap seconds close the discrepancy between the Earth’s rotation and UTC, their addition has posed challenges for technology companies, financial markets and other businesses that depend on precise timings.

In 2012, LinkedIn and Reddit crashed after the addition of a leap second. The same year, ticket bookings for Qantas, the Australian airline, collapsed after the leap second was added.

Three years later, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission also issued a warning against it. And in July 2022, engineers at Meta said : “Every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures.”

With pressure mounting, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which has the French acronym BIPM, voted in 2022 to scrap the leap second by 2035. But countries like Russia have wanted to push the implementation date back to 2040. Russia incorporates leap seconds directly into its GLONASS satellite-navigation system, so delaying the scrapping of leap seconds would buy Russia time to update its satellite systems.

Despite Moscow’s concern, the 69 member states of BIPM are now meeting on Thursday in Versailles outside Paris to debate and vote on a resolution to scrap the leap second by 2027.

According to the BIPM, the timekeeping authorities of countries around the world will discuss three proposals at Versailles.

First, they will consider whether atomic clocks are still the most accurate device when it comes to measuring what constitutes a second. Optical frequencies are now in fact more precise than atomic clocks. If a proposal to change how time is measured is accepted, the second might have a new definition, characterised by optical frequencies rather than the vibrations of atoms.

The second, most significant proposal pertains to dumping the leap second.

And finally, the third proposal on the table is a pitch to synchronise time measurements on Earth with a new time standard that NASA is developing for the moon.

Proposals that are accepted are expected to come into effect from May 20, 2027, World Metrology Day.

What happens if the leap second is scrapped?

If the leap second is scrapped, then it means our clocks will no longer be tied to the Earth’s rotation.

According to the NIST, if this happens, “then adjustments would have to be made to time stamps and legacy equipment and software which synchronise to UTC for astronomical observations.”

“Some proposals have been made to implement larger corrections like leap hours, which would occur much less often than leap seconds,” it added.

Scientists said human routines will not be impacted and software glitches, data server crashes and network failures for financial markets will be eliminated with the abandonment of leap seconds.

But over a period of centuries, the gap between the Earth’s cycle and our clocks will become more apparent: By 2100, clocks will be ahead of the Earth by 54 seconds. In another two millennia, that gap would have widened to several hours. The result? Sunrise and sunset times that would feel out of sync with people’s natural rhythms today.

articles.title: Justice Department cracks on America's 'North Korean employees problem'; says: More than 70 US companies affected, shares scammers email IDs
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced a coordinated crackdown on a North Korean remote IT worker scheme that allegedly infiltrated dozens of
articles.body: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced a coordinated crackdown on a North Korean remote IT worker scheme that allegedly infiltrated dozens of American companies using stolen identities, warning businesses about a growing threat that generated millions of dollars for Pyongyang. More than 70 US companies were affected by the operation, according to the department. The action includes criminal charges against multiple suspects, two arrests, searches of dozens of suspected "laptop farms" and the seizure of approximately 187 laptops and related devices used to help North Korean operatives obtain remote jobs at US companies.How the scheme workedAccording to an indictment unsealed in the Northern District of Ohio, North Korean workers got remote jobs at US companies from 2019 to around July 2025. They used stolen or fabricated identity documents, plus VPNs and proxy infrastructure, to appear to be U.S.-based employees.U.S.-based facilitators hosted the laptops that victim companies issued to these “employees” at their homes, the so-called laptop farms. They set up the machines, installed remote-access software and transferred the earnings to accounts controlled by North Korea.The scheme generated about $3 million in revenue, believed to have been sent to sanctioned North Korean entities. Victims included companies in health care, communications, cyber support, retail and manufacturing across Ohio, 16 other states and Washington, D.C.FBI raids laptop farmsAs part of the operation, the FBI executed searches at more than 40 locations in Texas believed to be connected to "laptop farms" used by North Korean workers. Investigators seized approximately 187 laptops and remote-access devices that allegedly enabled the fraud. The DOJ said the activity has been linked to a threat group known as "Famous Chollima," which has previously been associated with North Korean IT worker operationsArrests and chargesTwo US nationals, Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas, were arrested on charges of wire fraud, money laundering and identity theft. The indictment also names 10 China-based defendants, with two more under seal. The FBI said 14 people in total face charges.Texas raidsFrom Sept. 21 to Sept. 25, the FBI searched more than 40 residences in Texas in what it calls Operation Lonestar Roundup. Agents seized about 187 laptops and KVM devices. Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike identified the group as “Famous Chollima.”“Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould of the Northern District of Texas.Email IDs made publicThe department published 11 email addresses it says the operatives used and urged employers to add them to their screening indicators:Bright.star.me208@gmail.comMerrttank.bz@gmail.comrandyryang@gmail.commichaelb860102@gmail.comassassinki211@gmail.comdev.jerryyang@gmail.comdenis.turgenev2021@gmail.comyesiree.cano825@gmail.comthomasdenzelbrown@gmail.comanthonyortega4592@gmail.comtyler.j.palmi38@gmail.comChanging tacticsThe FBI issued a public service announcement with guidance for companies. It warns that North Korean workers increasingly recruit American facilitators to get around better detection. They give those facilitators a wider range of tasks and sometimes subcontract whole jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Some have also committed data extortion and stolen sensitive company data.A 2022 advisory said individual North Korean IT workers can earn up to $300,000 a year. articles.title: Backlash in Kashmir over proposal for uniform Friday sermons across mosques
articles.summary: Political and religious critics accuse India’s Modi government of curbing Kashmir’s freedom of religion and expression.
articles.body:
A proposed move by the Waqf Board in Indian-administered Kashmir to introduce uniform Friday sermons at mosques across the region has drawn backlash from politicians and religious leaders, who have accused the government of trying to assert control over Muslim religious spaces.

The Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board is headed by Darakshan Andrabi, a local leader associated with the Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, whose government stripped the region of its previous semi-autonomous status in 2019. Jammu and Kashmir was also partitioned into two federally governed territories, instead of functioning as a full-fledged state as it used to.

The board, which oversees Muslim religious endowments as mandated by Islamic laws, announced the controversial move last weekend, prompting a political controversy as the region’s top Muslim scholars slammed the proposal as “irresponsible interference into the religious affairs of Kashmiri Muslims”.

While defending the imposition of the uniform sermons, Andrabi told a leading Indian newspaper that a proposed committee formed under the board’s auspices “will be solely responsible for identifying the issue regarding the uniform sermon … [This step] is necessary to deal with issues in the [region], especially social evils, including drug abuse.”

Andrabi told the media that religious scholars will approve Friday sermons with no role for any government official in the decision.

On Sunday, the Waqf Board had summoned about 1500 top scholars and preachers from the Kashmir region. While some leaders were present at the venue, others from remote areas attended the meeting virtually.

A scholar from the mountainous Rajouri district, some 180km (110 miles) from the region’s biggest city of Srinagar, who had attended the meeting online, told Al Jazeera that Andrabi had passed instructions stating that only a pre-approved sermon drafted by a committee of senior-most scholars would be uniformly recited at the mosque pulpits on Fridays.

He said they were not told exactly who would be part of this committee.

“When we objected, saying that we won’t adhere to the directives if the sermon was found to be violative of Islamic teachings, she brushed aside our concerns and didn’t let us speak,” the scholar said on condition of anonymity as he feared reprisals by the authorities. “She [Andrabi] said that their decision was final as it had been four years in the making.”

A disputed region claimed by India and Pakistan, Kashmir has been at the centre of political turmoil for four decades. Years of peaceful demands for a referendum, to determine which country the Kashmiris would choose, transformed into an armed uprising against Indian rule in 1989 in response to allegations of election fixing.

In 2019, India scrapped the semi-autonomous status of Kashmir, imposing direct federal rule. The elections did not happen until 2024, when the local government was re-elected, albeit with a restricted mandate. De facto authority still rests with the New Delhi-appointed administrator.

The special conditions afforded under the erstwhile status had protected land and residency-related privileges while allowing Kashmiris to make their own laws.

One consequence of the 2019 decision was that Indigenous legal arrangements that governed the management of waqf, the charitable bequests that Muslims commit for the larger communal welfare, were replaced by those prevailing across India.

The new system gave broad powers to the federally controlled bureaucracy in the management of local religious boards such as waqf.

Since then, the Waqf Board has been accused multiple times by the local Kashmiri leaders of trying to undermine their religious freedoms or interfering with how the traditional religious practices have continued for generations.

“Centralised khutba or sermons used to take place in the name of a sultan or khalifa (Islamic caliph) during the medieval times. But that had sanctity because Kashmir was [then] an Islamic state. Today, we are supposed to be living in a secular state,” Nayeem Akhtar, a senior politician who served as Kashmir’s education minister during the previous elected government, when its special status was still operational, told Al Jazeera.

“As long as he has an audience, every cleric has freedom to speak about any topic of his choice. This freedom is enshrined in the very fundamentals of law,” he added.

Akhtar said the new instructions were coming from an office bearer associated with the BJP, which is why the latest move had provoked furious responses. “The board’s job is just managerial. It is exceeding its remit by trying to preach or guide the clerics on how they must do their job. Can a Muslim political party in India ever dictate how a Hindu pujari must conduct prayers or how a Christian pastor must deliver a sermon on Sunday?”

On Tuesday, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, the region’s top Muslim religious leader, cautioned that such a move would amount to “direct interference”.

The Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulema, a joint body of several religious organisations that he leads, said “determining sermon content was the responsibility of Islamic scholars and not of an administrative body.”

The condemnation was also shared by Omar Abdullah, the region’s elected head and member of the National Conference party that supports accession to India, albeit with the autonomous powers that New Delhi nullified seven years ago.

Following the backlash, the Waqf Board head Andrabi retracted her statement and said it had been left to the discretion of “independent scholars, preachers (and) sermonists” to talk about social issues such as rising suicides, mental trauma, substance abuse and more.

‘Exerting control on religious institutions’

This is not the first time that the BJP-led administration has been accused of trying to exert control over local religious institutions.

Earlier in January, Kashmiri Muslim scholars accused the government of discriminatory practices after the police distributed a four-page form titled “profiling of mosques” which sought intrusive details about the imams, muezzins and khatibs (preachers) of the mosques across the disputed region, including their biometric information.

For years, Muslim groups in the region have faced various restrictions on prayer, with Srinagar’s 600-year-old Jamia Masjid often being shut for important religious events such as Eid prayers or Laylat-al-Qadr, the most venerated night of the Islamic calendar, which falls in the month of Ramadan.

The administration argues these restrictions are imposed to ensure peace, but religious leaders insist that such prohibitory measures form a “systematic assault on the religious identity, dignity, and fundamental rights” of Kashmiri Muslims.

Farooq, the chief scholar, himself has been frequently subjected to such restrictions on his mobility, preventing him from giving Friday sermons on occasions when he is expected to speak on matters such as Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Previously, the Waqf Board has also sought to prohibit the practice of distributing yellow rice inside the compound of the major shrines in the region, a centuries-old tradition tied to the Sufi missionary councils that promoted Islam in Kashmir.

Religion has been a factor of political mobilisation

In 2022, the board also banned the age-old practice of collecting voluntary nazr-o-niyaz donations offered by devotees to the spiritual peers, mujawirs (attendants of a shrine) and khadims (caregivers). It cited the newly applicable federal laws as a reason for taking direct control over all financial collections and installing new donation boxes where all offerings went to the board.

Noor Ahmad Baba, a veteran Kashmiri political scientist and historian, said religion had always been a factor for political mobilisation in Kashmir, which is why attempts to manipulate or change the traditional religious arrangements evoke political outrage.

“The kind of political dispensation that we have and the kind of politics it has had with regard to Muslims is what makes the whole exercise suspicious,” Baba told Al Jazeera, referring to the BJP. “If the standardisation had come, for instance, from clerics with public acceptability, it wouldn’t have become an issue. No one can deny the need for religious leaders to talk about topics such as drug addiction, late marriages, climate change, social harmony and more.”

A Srinagar-based political analyst who has written about the conflict in Kashmir for four decades said such decisions reflected attempts to pre-emptively contain protests in Kashmir amid the rising wave of Hindu nationalism in India.

“A spate of recent mosque demolitions in cities such as Ujjain and Saharanpur in Uttar Pradesh showed how vehemently the far-right strains within India’s ruling apparatus were resurfacing,” the analyst told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. “This renewed communal posturing by the Modi regime was sufficient to provoke reactions in a place like Kashmir. The attempts to assert control over mosques must be seen in light of that.”

Kashmiri Muslim devotees pray on the last Friday of the Islamic holy fasting month of Ramadan at the Hazratbal Shrine in Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, on March 28, 2025 [Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto via Getty Images]

articles.title: Paul Bocuse gave his name to a French culinary school in 2002; eight years after his death, the institution now teaches about 1,200 students from 75 nationalities across a 17,000-square-metre campus in two castles
articles.summary: French chef Paul Bocuse lent his name to a culinary and hospitality school in 2002, helping shape an institution dedicated to preserving French gastronomy
articles.body: French chef Paul Bocuse lent his name to a culinary and hospitality school in 2002, helping shape an institution dedicated to preserving French gastronomy and the art of hospitality. Eight years after he died in 2018, the school, now known as Institut Lyfe, has grown into an international educational institution that says it welcomes 1,200 students from 75 nationalities across a 17,000-square-metre campus spread across two castles in Écully, near Lyon, France.According to the institute’s official website, the school offers programmes ranging from bachelor’s degrees to master’s and Master of Science (MSc) qualifications. Its teaching combines practical experience with project management, entrepreneurship and creativity, with the aim of preparing students for careers in culinary arts, restaurant management and hospitality.From a French culinary school to Institut Paul BocuseThe institution’s history dates to 1990, when the École des Arts Culinaires et d’Hôtellerie was inaugurated in Écully under the initiative of France’s then culture minister, Jack Lang, and with Bocuse serving as its honorary patron. Its stated objective was to promote French gastronomy internationally and pass on the country’s culinary traditions to future generations.Bocuse, one of France’s most influential chefs known as the 'Pope of Gastronomy', worked alongside Gérard Pélisson, co-founder of the Accor hotel group, to develop the school’s ambitions. In 1998, Pélisson took over as president of its governing body alongside Bocuse. Four years later, the institution adopted the name Institut Paul Bocuse, recognising the chef’s contribution and association with the school.Bocuse died on January 20, 2018, aged 91. His influence remains central to the institution’s identity, although the school changed its name to Institut Lyfe in 2023. The rebranding reflected its expanding international ambitions and a broader focus on culinary arts, hospitality and food service management.Two castles and an international student communityInstitut Lyfe describes its campus as a multicultural learning environment combining modern educational facilities with historic architecture. Its 17,000-square-metre campus encompasses two castles surrounded by landscaped grounds.The expansion includes Château de la Roseraie, which opened as a new centre for hospitality and management education in 2023, alongside the historic Château du Vivier campus. The newer centre added 22 classrooms, a 250-seat amphitheatre and collaborative workspaces, expanding the institution’s capacity and facilities. The institute says its student community represents 75 nationalities, giving it an international dimension while retaining its roots in the Lyon region, a major centre of French gastronomy.Its programmes span culinary arts, pastry, hospitality management, restaurant and wine management, and related specialisations. The teaching model emphasises practical learning, project-based work and entrepreneurial thinking, rather than limiting training to classroom instruction.Research, recognition and a Michelin-starred training restaurantThe institution has also expanded into research and higher education. In 1999, with support from Hervé Fleury and in partnership with Jean Moulin Lyon 3 University, it introduced a professional degree combining hospitality and cooking, which the institute describes as a first for a university programme portfolio.In 2008, it opened the Centre for Food and Hospitality Research, which the school identifies as the first of its kind in Europe. The centre was established to examine developments in food and hospitality and connect research with professional training.In 2018, Institut Paul Bocuse became the first private higher-education institution in hospitality and food service to receive dual recognition from the French state, according to its official history. This combined its existing professional certification with recognition from the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation. The institute subsequently secured state approval for its bachelor’s programmes.Its training restaurant, Saisons, received a Michelin star in 2020, adding another milestone to the school’s development. In 2022, Saisons became the first educational restaurant to join Relais & Châteaux, an international association of luxury hotels and restaurants, according to the institute.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 32 children and one teacher
articles.summary: Thirty-two children and a teacher were killed and dozens injured when the roof of a school in northern Pakistan collapsed on Thursday morning, authorities said.
articles.body: Thirty-two children and a teacher were killed and dozens injured when the roof of a school in northern Pakistan collapsed on Thursday morning, authorities said. Heavy overnight rainfall caused the roof of a two-story building at Al Khair Public School in the city of Peshawar to become unstable and later collapse, Bilal Ahmed of the local rescue services told CNN. The deceased children ranged in age from six to 14 years old, according to Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, where the victims were taken. A 25-year-old woman is also listed among the fatalities. Some children are still trapped in the rubble and rescuers are working to reach them, Ahmed said. Around 50 children were injured in the collapse, according to hospital figures. Several remain under medical observation. Video from the scene obtained by CNN showed ambulances rushing through narrow streets and crowds gathered outside the school building. Local residents were among the first people to reach the scene, and rescue workers arrived within minutes, eyewitnesses said. Building collapses are a common problem in Pakistan. Construction standards in the country are often poorly enforced, and many structures are built with substandard materials. Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari said the incident was a “heart-wrenching tragedy” and called for a comprehensive investigation into the cause of the deadly collapse. “In this hour of sorrow, the entire nation shares equally in the grief of the affected families,” the president’s office posted on X. The school’s owner has been arrested, and an investigation launched into the incident, a police official in Peshawar, Muhammad Ali, told CNN. The collapse comes just weeks after a fire tore through a hospital in the capital Islamabad, killing at least 14 newborns and sparking widespread anger and multiple arrests. The fire was confined to a third-floor nursery but officials said it spread so quickly that staff were able to rescue only one baby from among the 15 being cared for there. An inquiry found that the nursery had no fire alarm or sprinkler system and that the hospital lacked detailed procedures and training for responding to fires and other emergencies. In July, a roof collapse at a tutoring center under construction in Pakistan’s eastern city of Lahore killed at least 14 schoolchildren, police and rescue officials said at the time. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Trucks line up as long-delayed China-North Korea bridge officially opens
articles.summary: China and North Korea officially marked the long-delayed opening of their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of soured ties and pandemic-related disruptions to cross-border exchange.
articles.body: DANDONG, China — China and North Korea officially marked the long-delayed opening of their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of soured ties and pandemic-related disruptions to cross-border exchange. The area around the New Yalu River Bridge saw increased activity over the past few days, with trucks adorned with Chinese flags waiting on the bridge ahead of a crossing on Thursday. Crowds also gathered on the Chinese side along a road overlooking the bridge. Chinese and North Korean flags also lined the cable-stayed bridge with towering pylons that had been completed in 2014 but remained unused, while approach roads and a customs compound on the North Korea end remained unfinished. On Thursday, the countries held an opening ceremony for the new bridge, according to Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency. North Korea’s state media have yet to report on the scheduled event. The opening signals progress in bilateral relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, marked by two summit meetings between their leaders in the past year. China is by far Pyongyang’s largest trading partner, even after a series of U.N. sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers to and from North Korea over the country’s defiant missile and nuclear weapons development. China and Russia, two U.N. Security Council permanent member states that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans. Analysts said North Korea, despite the potential economic boost from active trade, remains cautious of greater dependence on China. Russia is accused by countries such as the U.S. and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang’s help in fighting the war in Ukraine. “The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade,” said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies in South Korea. But the bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for North Korea’s development projects, he said. China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3 billion last year, a 25% increase over the previous year. That was still well below levels before U.N. sanctions were tightened in 2017.

articles.body: A beach house on the Ben Buckler headland has sold for A$17.4 million. This is more than four times what the same property fetched in 2015. The mystery buyers of this laid-back coastal luxury home are a couple better known for their chicken than their real estate! Nando’s billionaire owner Richard ‘Dick’ Enthoven and his wife, Karen, are the buyers, according to a report by the Wentworth Courier.A quiet sale on a busy streetThe house sits at 148 Hastings Parade, in the stretch of North Bondi that is fast becoming a ‘billionaire’s row’, with Afterpay founder Nick Molnar, Australia’s youngest billionaire, living just up the road and Lorna Triguboff, the daughter of billionaire property developer Harry Triguboff, who is worth $32 billion, living further along.The sale of this four-bedroom beach house was completed on 20 June through a private treaty via Raine & Horne Double Bay. Ric Serrao handled the deal. Neither the agency nor the buyers have said much about the sale. The price itself is on the public record, which is how the details came to light.The mystery buyersRichard ‘Dick’ Enthoven and his wife, Karen, are the mystery buyers, according to the outlet. Richard is a South African billionaire who owns the Nando’s restaurant chain and the insurer Hollard. The settlement records show that the property is now registered in Karen Enthoven’s name. The previous owner was Adrian Reef, director of the corporate debt firm Reefine Capital.Inside the beach houseThis is not your regular beach shack. The beach house was designed by a leading Sydney architect and built by Pamment Projects, an award-winning builder. ‘This extraordinary freestanding residence sets a new benchmark for refined beachside living, where laid-back luxury and design excellence exist in perfect harmony,’ the listing says. The house has four bedrooms and three bathrooms.The house has changed hands only twice in 80 years, and the buyer gets a home built around how people actually live on the coast. The curated palette of European oak, timber and natural stone brings a beach-inspired aesthetic. The house is designed for year-round indoor and outdoor living and entertaining. It is divided into two separate indoor and outdoor zones, allowing a family to spread out without losing the feeling of being together. Soft, sandy tones keep the look relaxed, while the finishes remain polished. The north-facing backyard features a heated mosaic pool with jets, and both the front and rear alfresco areas catch the ocean breeze. The rear barbecue runs directly off the gas mains, making weekend cooking easy. The expansive ocean-view terrace, with its resort-style back garden, also makes the property perfect for buyers seeking a laid-back, luxurious home.Inside, every bedroom has a built-in wardrobe, air conditioning and ceiling fans. The main suite looks out over the water and features a freestanding bath and a rain shower. Skylights fill the custom study and the rest of the home with daylight. Zellige tiles and heated floors feature in the laundry and bathrooms. The house is designed with comfort and safety in mind. Daikin zoned air conditioning, an Escea gas fireplace, ceiling-mounted Sonos speakers and an alarm system are among its features. The Caesarstone kitchen has gas appliances, two Bosch dishwashers, an island breakfast bar with a wine fridge tucked underneath, and a full butler’s pantry.A rear gate opens onto the North Bondi golf course and its walking tracks, while the garage has room for three cars, plus storage or a man cave. From there, the village cafés, cliff walks and Bondi Beach are all within easy reach.Meanwhile, the Enthovens already own Greenoaks Cottage, a nine-bedroom 1850s mansion in Darling Point. They bought it in late 2019 for $18 million from Anne-Maree Kerry, a former Olympic gymnast, and Phil Kerry, the boss of recruitment firm K2.The couple also owned a waterfront home in Point Piper, which sold for $21.8 million to developer Barrie Nesbitt and his wife, Emma. articles.title: Pope Leo had a good night in the hospital, the Vatican says
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV, recovering from surgery for lung cancer, had a good night in the hospital and has eaten breakfast, the Vatican said Thursday.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV, recovering from surgery for lung cancer, had a good night in the hospital and has eaten breakfast, the Vatican said Thursday. Leo, 71, has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung in a surgery on Tuesday afternoon. The Vatican has said the surgery was completed successfully, without complications. It has not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. Further updates are expected on Thursday, but the pope’s pathology report may not be available for several days. Leo‘s public schedule has been canceled until October 20. The pope’s doctors have so far given no indication that he might need further treatment. The Vatican has also not indicated whether Leo’s cancer might have spread. In the meantime, the Vatican released its first post-surgery message from the pope. “As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” read the message, which was addressed to the participants at a meeting to mark the 10th anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia,” a 2016 document on Catholic doctrine released by Pope Francis. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church,” the message read. As Leo continues with recovery, his brother, Louis Prevost, is being treated for blood cancer, a source close to the family told NBC Chicago. Prevost said they’re optimistic the pope will rally. “They caught it early enough, and he’ll be able to heal from the surgery and go on with his papal ministry,” he said in an interview with Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty. Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they removed from his right lung. Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.

articles.title: Imran Khan: Bollywood actor asked to leave India after participating in CJP protest in Mumbai
articles.summary: The Bollywood actor had been detained and released while participating in a protest in Mumbai on 10 October.
articles.body:
Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms.

An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections.

"Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday.

Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court.

Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting.

But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest.

The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic".

Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na.

He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992.

Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly.

The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade.

On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges.

"Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement.

The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India".

Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest.

"I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said.

He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation.

Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters.

He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform.

Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call.

On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi.

On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.

The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital.

articles.title: Riots erupt in Albania’s capital as students join anti-government movement
articles.summary: Protesters in Albania attacked government buildings, banks, businesses and other sites during riots that lasted more than eight hours across the capital Tirana on Wednesday in a violent escalation of an anti-government movement that has staged rallies for months.
articles.body: Protesters in Albania attacked government buildings, banks, businesses and other sites during riots that lasted more than eight hours across the capital Tirana on Wednesday in a violent escalation of an anti-government movement that has staged rallies for months. Hundreds of youths smashed store fronts, set fires and caused damage to at least four government ministry buildings during running battles with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon to try and hold back the crowds. Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries, while 35 people were detained. President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.” The latest demonstrations, continuing for a second day, were organized by student groups seeking education reforms. But the protesters have joined a broader anti-government campaign opposed to a development project linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The so-called flamingo movement is calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama over allegations of widespread corruption. The movement earned the name after protesters used signs depicting the pink bird. Rallies staged for months against the proposed coastal project have fueled political tensions in Albania, which is aspiring to join the European Union. It has struggled with repeated bouts of instability since the collapse of a harsh communist regime in the early 1990s. On Wednesday, officers in riot gear clashed with youths who dismantled police cordons and set up their own street barricades using burning trash bins. Police struggled to cope with the multiple outbreaks of violence. Health Minister Klodiana Spahiu, who visited the injured officers in hospital, called the violence “intolerable.” The EU delegation in Albania called for a proportionate response from authorities following protest organizers’ “allegations of excessive violence by the police against protestors and journalists.” “We express concern on the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana,” the delegation said. “Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values.”

articles.title: Crew in Lewis fishing boat tragedy named by police
articles.summary: The alarm was raised after the men's fishing boat failed to return as planned to Lewis on Tuesday.
articles.body:
A fisherman whose body was found after a boat went missing off the Western Isles on Tuesday has been named as Douglas Craigie.

The 49-year-old's crew-mates, Norman Murray, who is 40 and known as Tam, and 23-year-old Murdo Morrison are still missing.

The three men, who are all from Lewis, had been fishing in a boat called Kilda.

The vessel disappeared during stormy weather off Port of Ness in north Lewis.

The search for the missing crew and boat has resumed after being suspended overnight.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said aircraft and coastguard teams were involved.

Police Scotland said it was believed the fishermen had sailed from Brevaig in Lewis at about 07:30 on Tuesday before travelling to the Port of Ness area to fish.

The Kilda was reported overdue at about 21:20 on Tuesday.

Extensive searches were conducted on Wednesday despite bad weather, with gale-force winds.

The body of Douglas Craigie was recovered in the Port of Ness area at about 02:45 on Wednesday.

Ch Insp Ross McCartney, local area commander for the Western Isles, said: "Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragic incident.

"The families of all three men involved are being provided with specialist support as our searches continue. We would ask that the privacy of the families of all three men are respected at this difficult time."

He added: "We are working closely with the HM Coastguard and RNLI to search for the vessel and the two missing men

"We know that the local community will be keen to help in any way they can.

"However, conditions are very challenging and I would urge people not to put themselves at any risk. Please do not attempt to carry out searches in areas which put you at risk of harm.

"Instead, if you believe you may have any information which could assist emergency services then please call 101 quoting reference 3575 of 13 October."

McCartney said a police presence would remain in the Port of Ness area.

A spokesperson for the MCA said: "A range of search and rescue assets have been sent in response, including HM Coastguard helicopters and aeroplanes, coastguard rescue teams, lifeboats, and a nearby vessel.

The search is taking place off Ness, a sparsely populated area on the northern tip of Lewis.

It is an area of rugged coastline, with many of its roughly 1,300 people living in crofting townships - small holdings where families can raise livestock and grow crops while working other jobs.

The parish has one of the highest concentrations of Gaelic speakers in the Western Isles.

A minute's silence was held earlier at the Royal National Mòd, Scotland's annual celebration of Gaelic culture and language, which is taking place in Glasgow.

Speaking at Westminster, Western Isles MP Torcuil Crichton paid tribute to coastguard, RNLI and police teams searching for the missing crew.

He said: "The Western Isles have been struck this week by maritime tragedy by the sinking of the fishing vessel, Kilda, in a Tuesday night storm off the coast of Lewis with what is feared to be the subsequent loss of three souls abroad."

Crichton said his condolences went to the families involved, and to other fishing communities that had suffered losses over the years.

On Wednesday, Kenneth Macleod, convener of local authority Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, told BBC Radio Scotland's Lunchtime Live programme : "It is a very dark day for the community of Ness and the community of Lewis in general.

"Our thoughts and condolences are with the families affected.

"We cannot comprehend what the families of the three fishermen are going through at the moment."

In a message on X, First Minister John Swinney said: "This is deeply distressing news.

"My heart goes out to the families of the three fishermen in Ness, and the communities on the Isle of Lewis."

articles.title: Shakira was only 20 when she launched her education mission in Colombia; nearly three decades later, her foundation reports supporting more than 300 public schools
articles.summary: In Colombia, a school can mean more than a place to attend lessons.
articles.body: In Colombia, a school can mean more than a place to attend lessons. For families living in neighbourhoods where public services and safe facilities have been limited, the condition of a classroom can shape a child's daily life. Shakira began directing her attention towards education early in her music career, establishing a charitable foundation in 1997, when she was 20. The work eventually extended beyond individual donations to the construction of schools in communities where children had few suitable places to learn. Nearly three decades later, her education initiative remains part of her public work, with the wider school-building effort associated with hundreds of educational facilities and thousands of students across Colombia.Shakira’s education mission began with a foundation for Colombia’s underserved childrenShakira's involvement in education dates back to 1997, when she established the Pies Descalzos Foundation (Barefoot Foundation). Born in Barranquilla on Colombia's Caribbean coast, the singer was still in the early stages of her rise to international fame. Her charitable work developed alongside her music career, with a particular emphasis on children who faced barriers to education.The foundation's approach has included building schools and supporting educational opportunities in underserved communities. Rather than concentrating solely on financial assistance, its projects have sought to provide facilities where children can study and take part in activities beyond the classroom. In an interview with America’s Quarterly, Shakira said, “The goal of my philanthropic work has always been to make sure that every child has a chance to live up to his or her potential. That means our work won’t be done until every child has access to quality education from early childhood to adulthood.”The $10 million school Shakira helped bring to a Colombian communityAs reported by SBSNews, one example of the foundation's work came in March 2014, when Shakira travelled to Lomas de Peyé, a low-income neighbourhood in Cartagena, to open a newly built school. The visit brought attention to the conditions in which local children had previously studied and to the role a purpose-built facility could play in the area.Reportedly, the school covered approximately 8,000 square metres and was reported to have cost around $10 million. Funding came from a combination of local and international donors, alongside money from Shakira herself. Its facilities included a football pitch and classrooms designed to accommodate about 1,700 students.The previous school building had raised concerns about safety, particularly during strong winds coming in from the Caribbean. The new brick structure offered a more substantial setting for lessons and provided facilities for activities outside the regular school day.At the opening, Patricia Sierra, then director of the foundation, described the project as a community centre as well as a school. The ambition was to make the grounds available for informal learning, sport, arts and gatherings, potentially reaching around 5,000 people through these wider programmes, as reported by World Economic Forum (WEF).From an early commitment to a wider networkBy the time of the 2014 inauguration, the Cartagena school was described by the Australian Associated Press report published by SBS News as the sixth school built by Shakira's foundation in Colombia. The Pies Descalzos Foundation reports supporting more than 300 public schools across Colombia, benefiting over 282,160 children and young people. However, that figure does not mean the charity built 300 schools from the ground up. Its official website separately records 22 schools built or renovated in Colombia, distinguishing its construction work from its broader support for existing public schools.The programme also reflects the way Shakira has used her public profile to support causes outside the entertainment industry.Education remains central to Shakira's charitable workAt the Cartagena opening, Shakira argued that education should be treated as a right rather than a privilege. Her remarks placed the responsibility for children's education not only on charities and individual donors but also on the state.Shakira's foundation began its work when she was 20, before the singer had reached the height of her international commercial success. Its subsequent school projects have made education a long-running part of her philanthropic activities in Colombia.Nearly three decades after Shakira established the Pies Descalzos Foundation in 1997, the organisation continues to support education in underserved Colombian communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cornell president pressed by faculty over handling of fraternity rape allegations
articles.summary: Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff faced angry members of the school’s faculty Wednesday at a meeting that underscored deep frustration over his administration’s handling of a woman’s report that she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
articles.body: ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff faced angry members of the school’s faculty Wednesday at a meeting that underscored deep frustration over his administration’s handling of a woman’s report that she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024. Kotlikoff acknowledged some missteps, but also defended his leadership as he took questions from the university’s Faculty Senate before it debated a no-confidence resolution in his administration. The meeting was closed to the media, but in an audio recording obtained by The Associated Press, Kotlikoff asked for more time to implement reforms and push for cultural changes in student social life. He insisted experienced leadership was necessary to confront problems “that are not simplistic, they’re not easy, they can’t be brushed aside with a wave of a hand.” Replacing a president isn’t the right way to address the situation and would harm Cornell’s reputation, Kotlikoff said. Kotlikoff also left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life, saying Cornell needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely. On Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced a ban on fraternity parties through the end of the academic year. “If, at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment and we can’t be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision,” he said, adding that the university should rely on research and evidence rather than emotion. After Kotlikoff departed, a string of faculty speakers said they had lost confidence in the administration’s ability to combat sexual assault on campus. “The faculty were extremely angry. They gave him a hard time, I think appropriately so,” said Richard Bensel, a professor of government. Some Faculty Senate members warned that a hasty no-confidence vote would do little to address the underlying problems. Debate was expected to continue Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting. A no-confidence vote by the faculty would be largely symbolic, but could send a message to the university’s trustees, who ultimately decide how the university is run and who leads it. Accuser’s lawsuit has roiled campus A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved. The criminal investigation by Cornell’s police department stalled after the local district attorney quickly decided that no crime had occurred. At the time, Kotlikoff publicly addressed what he called “deeply disturbing” allegations, suspended the fraternity and said criminal and university investigations were underway. He subsequently convened a presidential task force to examine how Cornell handles sexual assault. But in an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what had happened to the woman or the criminal investigation. Asked by a faculty member whether he read the Cornell Police Department’s report on the rape allegations, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he had not, but said that was because the police investigation was confidential and university policy is that top administrators shouldn’t have a role in criminal investigations. “I really reject the idea that I had no interest in it or was not concerned about it,” Kotlikoff said. Kotlikoff denied that he wasn’t aware that students had been expelled or suspended as a result of the university’s Title IX investigation, but acknowledged that, until recently, he didn’t know the woman had dropped out of Cornell. Faculty describe ‘contentious’ meeting “The institution is split in significant ways,” said Grant Farred, professor of Africana Studies and English, describing those in the humanities as feeling they had enough information to proceed while those in the sciences wanted more data. Iris Packman, a research and policy expert at Cornell’s Climate Jobs Institute, said she felt Kotlikoff got “defensive.” Labor history professor Paul Ortiz, lead sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, said the debate was animated by the perception that the administration wasn’t doing enough to address “a perpetual ongoing crisis.” Anne Marie Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations, said she welcomed Kotlikoff’s recent announcement that state police, rather than campus police, will temporarily handle investigations of sexual assaults, but she questioned the timing, a day before the Senate debate. Professor who reported harassment says it nearly cost her career For Ariana Kim, an associate music professor at Cornell, Kotlikoff’s acknowledgment that he had not followed up on the woman’s case was “appalling.” A Grammy-nominated violinist, Kim told The Associated Press that when she first started at Cornell a decade ago, she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues. Cornell, she said, failed to properly document her complaints and never clearly informed her of what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken. “I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation,” she said. Kim said her efforts to avoid colleagues who had harassed her later became a point of criticism during her tenure review. In one instance, a professor cited her unwillingness to accept his advice and her avoidance of him when he voted against granting her tenure. Kotlikoff became the university’s interim president in July 2024 and took the job permanently last year. He’s faced challenges including a dining and custodial workers strike, ire over his decision last year to pay $60 million to settle Trump administration civil rights investigations, and accusations from activists that his administration stifled campus protests.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan make first joint appearance since returning to the UK
articles.summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have made their first joint public appearance in Britain since moving back to the country.
articles.body: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have made their first joint public appearance in Britain since moving back to the country. Prince Harry and Meghan were greeted by well-wishers as they arrived at the Community Recording Studio (CRS) in Nottingham on Thursday morning. Crowds gave the couple balloons and flowers, Britain’s PA Media news agency reported, with Harry and Meghan stopping to greet onlookers and pose for selfies. Meghan told one woman in the crowd: “It’s great to be back.” The CRS is a charity that teaches film, video and music skills to young people. Inside the studio, Meghan joined a group of girls for a confidence-building and bracelet-making workshop. When asked what makes them feel most like themselves, one participant said she liked doing gymnastics, to which Meghan replied: “Our daughter is doing that too right now. She loves it,” according to PA Media. The duchess, whose Netflix lifestyle “With Love, Meghan” show centered around hosting and cooking, added: “I feel most like myself when I’m with my family and also when I’m cooking. I love doing that. I love to cook.” In a surprise announcement this summer, the couple revealed that they would be leaving their home in California to resettle in the UK, together with their two children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. The family landed in August, ahead of the start of the school year last month. They returned as private citizens and are not resuming any official duties on behalf of King Charles III. The engagement – the first of a few scheduled for Thursday – comes more than six years after the couple departed the United Kingdom for the United States and the years since have seen a public falling out with some members of the royal family. Harry and Meghan had cited tabloid intrusion, racism in British institutions, online abuse and complex family dynamics as among the reasons behind their 2020 departure. This is not the duke’s first time at CRS. He visited the studio in September last year and announced a personal donation of £1.1 million ($1.45 million) to Children in Need to assist the charity’s work tackling violence affecting young people. Harry and Meghan’s visit is not an official royal engagement. Last month, Harry’s father, King Charles, issued a letter in which he clarified that the couple should be treated as “private citizens.” The missive is said to have caught the Sussexes off guard. According to the letter, sent by the UK’s Lord Chamberlain – the most senior officer of the British royal household – all charitable work carried out by Harry and Meghan is a “personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.” The letter also made clear that any operational issues involving them should be directed to the relevant police authorities. Harry has continued to push for the UK Home Office to reinstate his family’s taxpayer-funded security, which was downgraded when the family left for North America in 2020. The last time the Sussexes appeared together in public in Britain was four years ago, at the funeral of Harry’s grandmother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, in September 2022. While living in the US, Harry made several trips back to the UK, including for the funeral of his grandmother Queen Elizabeth II in 2022 and the coronation of his father King Charles III the following year. CNN’s Lauren Said-Moorhouse and Max Foster contributed reporting.

articles.title: Meghan makes first official public appearance since moving back to UK
articles.summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are taking part in a series of events linked to their charitable work in Nottingham.
articles.body:
The Duchess of Sussex has made her first official public appearance since moving back to the UK, telling well-wishers "it's great to be back".

Meghan arrived at a youth charity in Nottingham alongside her husband, the Duke of Sussex, on Thursday morning. The pair, who are also expected to visit a food bank later, hugged and posed for selfies with the public.

The duchess spoke to a number of people in the crowd, telling one "we got lucky" as they chatted about the weather.

She has shared glimpses of her life back in the UK on social media, but this is the first time she has attended any public events since the family returned from California.

During a bracelet-making workshop, Meghan disclosed her daughter Princess Lilibet had been enjoying a new hobby.

When one youngster told the duchess she liked doing gymnastics, Meghan replied: "Oh yeah. Our daughter is doing that too right now. She loves it."

Later, she gave the young girls some advice on building confidence.

"We have to remember to talk to ourselves like we talk to our best friends," she said. "It's really important to be just as kind to yourself."

A spokesperson for Harry and Meghan said Nottingham is "a special place" for them both, as it is where they made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.

The pair are attending these events not as working royals, but as public figures and supporters of the projects they're visiting.

The Royal Household has made it clear they view them as private citizens.

Despite that, Thursday’s schedule has a distinctly royal feel to it.

The first stop on their visit to Nottingham is the Community Recording Studio, a charity which Prince Harry has been supporting since 2013.

Its CEO Trevor Rose told the BBC they only found out about the trip a few weeks ago, and could not believe it.

"It's exciting times. Completely random, phoned, mentioned a idea, said they'd like to come down," he said.

"I thought it was going to be something in the future, next thing I know it's two weeks later and we are here, so yeah it's a complete shock."

A group of fans had built up steadily throughout the morning, some carrying flowers whilst one child has a unicorn balloon.

Later in the day, the pair are expected to visit Himmah Hub, a local charity tackling food poverty, where they will observe cooking classes taking place and help to prepare food parcels.

Their third engagement is at Epic Partners, a group working to support young people through youth work, sport and mentoring.

The couple have a private security team with them in Nottingham and local police teams are understood to be aware of their visit.

Harry and Meghan's spokesperson told BBC News they were "really excited" to be back together in Nottingham, nine years since their last joint visit.

"They are back here primarily because they support and believe in the organisations they are visiting.

"They enjoy coming back to revisit projects they are personally invested in, to meet the same people and understand what is happening and how things are changing."

In 2017, Harry and Meghan visited Nottingham's Lace Market before a visit to a World Aids Day charity fair.

Pictures from that trip showed the couple smiling as they met enthusiastic crowds.

The pair and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, returned to the UK in August after living in the US for six years.

They have reportedly settled in the Cotswolds, and their children have moved schools after issues were raised by their security team about the school run.

It also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is reconsidering Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

The Sussexes will not be spending Christmas with the King at the traditional royal family gathering at Sandringham, Norfolk. BBC News understands that they are likely to spend it privately with Meghan's mother Doria Ragland.
