articles.title: What we know about Katie Zacharia’s legal work in China
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia gave a surprising answer when asked on Tuesday where she passed the bar exam: “When I moved to China,” she told reporters. Whether Zacharia passed the bar exam at all is in growing doubt. A watchdog group filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California asking it…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia gave a surprising answer when asked on Tuesday where she passed the bar exam: “When I moved to China,” she told reporters.

Whether Zacharia passed the bar exam at all is in growing doubt. A watchdog group filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California asking it to investigate whether she broke the law by claiming to practice law.

Zacharia received a law degree from Pepperdine University Caruso School of Law in 2011, but the Popular Information newsletter reported that she is not licensed to practice law in the U.S. or Washington, D.C.

The White House has not provided any evidence to prove otherwise.

Zacharia’s LinkedIn says she was “general counsel” of Fix California — an organization started by Richard Grenell, a former Trump administration official — from January 2024 to March 2025 and that she was an “associate” on the International Practice Team for Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013.

The Hill has reached out to both organizations for comment.

The White House said Zacharia moved to China with her husband after graduating law school and worked in international transaction law. She told NewsNation that she practiced “with all the appropriate credentials.”

Experts told The Hill that even if Zacharia worked at a law firm in China, that didn’t necessarily make her a lawyer.

“I don’t believe that she could have taken the Chinese bar exam — American citizens are not, by rule, allowed to sit for it, and there’s no apparent reason to believe that she could have made some special arrangement (if she did, I’d love to learn how she managed that, as it would be extremely difficult),” Taisu Zhang, a professor at Yale Law School who works on contemporary Chinese law and politics, wrote to The Hill.

“It is possible, however, to do some international transaction-related legal work without ever having passed a bar exam,” he wrote. “Many international law firms allow junior associates to begin work on transactional work without having passed a bar exam but will limit the tasks they can perform until they do.”

He added that there’s usually a certain period of time that people can work at law firms in China without having passed the bar until they’re forced to leave.

“But until that grace period runs out, she could have been working at an international law firm without any bar admission,” he said.

Donald Clarke, a professor at George Washington University School of Law and a specialist in Chinese law, pointed The Hill to a specific provision in Chinese law that says a person must be of Chinese nationality to take the bar exam.

“To the best of my knowledge, Zacharia has never claimed to be a Chinese national,” Clarke said.

Mark Jia, a law professor at Georgetown University who is a scholar of comparative and transactional law, wrote on social platform X that “the work category Zacharia likely had in a China was ‘foreign legal consultant,’ typically reserved for foreign trained lawyers working at Chinese law firms who are limited to advising on foreign and international law.”

While he noted that the rules may have been different when she was employed between 2011 and 2013, he said, “It is possible that she wasn’t barred anywhere when she took on this role, though I have to imagine this was somewhat rare even back then.”

Judd Legum, the journalist behind Popular Information, pointed out multiple examples of Zacharia referring to herself as a lawyer on television.

The Campaign for Accountability, which filed the complaint in California, notes that if Zacharia has “repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so,” then she may have violated state law.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has,” Campaign for Accountability Executive Director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement.

President Trump also referred to Zacharia as an attorney when he announced that she would be the new press secretary.

“Katie is a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax,” he wrote on Truth Social last week.

A State Bar of California spokesperson told The Hill that it had “no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black (or each with Katie) having been licensed to practice law in California.” Zacharia’s maiden name is Black.

White House communications director Steven Cheung attacked the watchdog group as a “radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls” in a social media post Wednesday, but he did not offer any new information on his colleague’s legal qualifications.

articles.title: Wales' national poet says royal visit poem rejection is 'concerning'
articles.summary: Hanan Issa's poem To Grow, referring to Gaza and trans healthcare, was rejected from the ceremony.
articles.body:
Wales' national poet has said it is "quite concerning" that a poem raising political issues was rejected from the Senedd's opening ceremony.

Briefings to the media about the event said a poetry reading would be made by Hanan Issa at the ceremony on Thursday, which will be attended by King Charles III and Queen Camilla.

But on Wednesday, Issa posted on social media that the poem she submitted, To Grow, which referred to Gaza and trans healthcare, was rejected on the grounds that the ceremony was "apolitical".

The Senedd Commission said the poem, that Issa had reworked and had already been translated into Welsh, was "not the right fit for this occasion".

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast , Issa said she would not be attending the ceremony where King Charles and the Queen will officially open the Senedd's seventh term.

The poet added: "I am not welcome anymore. I won't be part of the ceremony."

The first minister will be among those greeting the King on the Senedd steps with the presiding officer Huw Irranca-Davies and the Labour Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, who will represent the UK government.

Issa said the feedback received was that the poem had an "edge" and could "perhaps be softened."

"That's what I thought I'd done and obviously, it wasn't enough," she said.

Issa added it was "telling" that in the chamber where political issues are discussed "a poem that raises political issues is not welcome, that feels quite concerning".

The Welsh-Iraqi poet, filmmaker, and artist said she was inspired by Welsh poet Saunders Lewis' imagery of Wales as a vineyard, and developed that around the brief's request.

"The brief asked for something that celebrated members and their achievements, and something that served as a reminder of their commitment to the people of Wales.

"I don't know about you, but celebrating the achievements of members when they are just about to be sworn in feels a bit premature."

Instead, Issa decided to write something to remind the politicians of "their commitment".

"I wrote something that described Wales as a garden, and our Assembly Members as its gardeners."

Issa said that after submitting the first version she could have refused to make changes, but instead chose to compromise and try to find a halfway point.

A second version used "more abstract language", Issa said, but it was also rejected.

Based on the brief, Issa said it didn't sound like "they want a poem just about daffodils, and so it felt like a disservice to write something that was quite surface level".

"We've just faced a summer of wildfires. We're going into a season, no doubt, of floods. The proposed data centres, people have lots of concerns about that.

"There's so many things, and so it felt important for me to speak to those things."

Quoting John Lennon, Issa said: "'A poet's role is to try to express how people are feeling' and it felt like an important moment to do that."

The Senedd Commission said: "After a development process, we concluded that the poem was not the right fit for this occasion."

It added: "We respect the National Poet of Wales' artistic independence and continue to admire and value their work."

Also speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, Irranca-Davies described Issa as a "fantastic poet" and said it was "disappointing" for her not to have her poem there, but added it had been "deemed not appropriate for this occasion".

He said: "I think the reason that's been made clear by the Senedd Commission is there's plenty of debate and political debate, not just in Wales, but within the Senedd day in, day out, week in, week out, and that's a really good thing, that robust debate on difficult issues."

He said the ceremonial opening was not a day for political debate, but a chance to mark the start of the Senedd term.

"It's the one day of the term when this official opening, when we come together to pause, mark the start of the Senedd, celebrate the communities of Wales, remind members of their service to the people of Wales that they serve, and there will be many fantastic performances here today as well," he added.

Reform sources said they felt the commission made the correct call.

Literature Wales said the National Poet's role was to use "poetry to inspire reflection, conversation and positive change."

It added: "We are disappointed that this formal celebration of Welsh democracy will not include a literary contribution but accept the Senedd Commission's decision."

articles.title: Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
articles.summary: Houthis attempt to raise the cost of the Yemen war for Saudi Arabia as attacks, fighting intensify.
articles.body:
Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.

Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.

He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.

A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.

Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.

Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?

Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.

Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.

Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.

Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.

Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.

The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.

Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.

Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.

Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”

“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.

What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?

Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “ Dawn of Yemen “, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait , a vital maritime trade chokepoint.

The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.

On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.

The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.

Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.

Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.

The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.

Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.

“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.

The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.

The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast ⁠are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than ⁠700 casualties in a single week.

articles.title: Some GOP walk the line on Trump’s tariffs and a look at Apple HomeView: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Some Republican candidates are putting distance between themselves and Trump’s tariff policies.
articles.body: Some Republican candidates are putting distance between themselves and Trump’s tariff policies. Ukraine defies the U.S. president to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries. And a look at Apple’s new HomeView device, which is part iPad, part Apple Watch and part CarPlay. Here’s what to know today. Some Republicans in key races break with Trump over tariffs In a handful of battleground races, Republican candidates are speaking out against tariffs, President Donald Trump’s marquee economic policy. They’re seeking a middle ground, knowing the cost of living is a top voter concern. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Those voicing their concerns on the campaign trail include Senate candidates Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire and former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan. Gubernatorial candidates with doubts over the policy include Rep. John James in Michigan and Pennsylvania state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. America’s trade war with Canada is a particular concern for Collins and Rogers, who say they’ve spoken to Cabinet officials to get the administration to make a deal or exempt specific items from a list of tariffed goods. Their Democratic rivals are hitting back, saying the efforts have either not gone far enough or are self-serving in the final weeks of the campaign. How GOP strategists reacted to the candidates’ split with Trump. Americans are almost evenly split over which party they think would do a better job of handling the economy, a recent NBC News polling average shows, with 39% preferring Democrats and 38% preferring Republicans. See the poll results here. Plus, see an overview of this year’s biggest elections in our Countdown to midterms, as well as breakdowns of Trump’s approval rating, important state races and early voting. More politics news: Federal agents have seized Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone and subpoenaed her family members as part of an investigation into potential immigration-related crimes. For subscribers: Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed spoke about the Iran war, the economy and the issues driving the competitive Michigan Senate race in an exclusive interview with “NBC Nightly News” anchor Tom Llamas. For subscribers: Republican groups have pulled millions of dollars in ads from some battleground House races while pouring money into others. Here’s which races took the biggest hits — and why. Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries as anger mounts with Trump Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of the “dangerous” withdrawal of intelligence sharing and restrictions on the Starlink internet services. Kyiv held off on attacks for three days after Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, but accused Russia of repeatedly violating the truce with attacks on its power grid. Trump has blamed the Ukrainian campaign for fueling a rise in energy prices, despite the impact of his own war with Iran. Ukrainian officials and military units accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling a technology at the heart of their battlefield communications and drone operations. Kyiv sees this as an attempt to pressure it into concessions by hampering its aerial defense and military operations. Overnight, Musk said it was “time for Zelenskyy to go.” In an interview with the Financial Times, published today, Zelenskyy indicated his own patience had been exhausted. “The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying. Hours later a fire was reported at an oil refinery in the western Ryazan region, Gov. Pavel Malkov said. More on what Ukraine’s resumption of strikes means for the war. Apple’s HomeView is part iPad, part Apple Watch and part CarPlay Apple introduced HomeView this week — a “FrankenApple creation,” as NBC News chief tech analyst Joanna Stern calls it, that combines elements of the Apple Watch, an iPad and the iPhone’s CarPlay functionality onto a $299 device. It’s the company’s answer to Amazon’s Echo Show and Google’s Nest Hub. Here are the basics: The HomeView has a 7-inch-square Liquid Retina touchscreen that includes a 12-megapixel camera for FaceTime and mirror mode. Widgets can be customized like an Apple Watch. And it can recognize six people, presumably family members. Notably, users will need to have an iPhone or an iPad to even use the HomeView in the first place. But, Stern writes, “for those of us who have Apple HomeKit gear all over our homes, this new product might just be… a good idea?” Read Stern’s full analysis here. Roller-coaster death exposes lack of federal oversight Days after a roller-coaster death this week at Six Flags Over Georgia, preliminary findings suggest that 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was “ejected” from the Goliath ride and fell to his death, according to the Cobb County Police Department. The ride remains closed, and nine similar rides have been temporarily shut down across Six Flags’ North American parks. The incident in Georgia, combined with recent allegations that some people who rode the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California suffered “catastrophic” brain injuries, shed light on the lack of federal oversight for amusement park rides. A 1980s court ruling stripped the U.S. Product Safety Commission of its power to oversee rides at “fixed-site parks.” Since then, a disjointed network of state regulations and voluntary industry guidelines has sprouted in its place. While safety standards have been adopted, experts say they’re voluntary, and every state takes different approaches when it comes to compliance. What to know before riding a roller coaster. Staff Pick: Americans’ eating habits are changing. For Chick-fil-A, adapting to them is a tall order. Chick-fil-A is a company that cherishes its past. The recipe for its signature chicken sandwich hasn’t changed in 60 years. It has been a private, family-owned business from the very beginning. But Chick-fil-A and the fast-food industry broadly are contending with a changing consumer. People are eating in and consuming less as rising costs squeeze Americans’ budgets and as GLP-1s shrink people’s appetites. A restaurant industry expert told me you’d expect fast-food spots to benefit from consumers who are cutting back on spending. But that’s not what we’re seeing. Foot traffic at fast-food restaurants from January through September this year is 2% lower than during the same period last year. And yet foot traffic at Chick-fil-A is 5.7% higher. So what’s Chick-fil-A’s secret sauce? articles.title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
articles.summary: It is the "backbone of military communications in Ukraine" that provides vital high-speed internet to forces across the country.
articles.body:
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.

For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.

Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.

But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection . This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.

The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless.

"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."

Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.

The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.

It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.

It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.

While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade service, designed for use by the Pentagon.

Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.

The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February , giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.

How does Starlink work on a battlefield?

Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".

This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield.

"It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme.

"It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added.

The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.

In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.

It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC.

Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added.

Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.

For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal".

With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.

While Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it.

Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine.

"If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024.

But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not.

During a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky had said he hoped it was just a mistake, however, in a later interview with the Financial Times, he said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will."

Musk said that Starshield is managed by the US government and suggested the Pentagon could be responsible.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X . "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the president of the United States]."

He added: "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."

The BBC has contacted the White House and Pentagon for comment.

The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that left 600,000 without power and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.

"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.

Relations between the US and Ukraine have worsened recently, especially since the US announced a deal with Russia to import its diesel into the American market.

Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and in response Donald Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".

On Sunday, Trump announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, but three days later, Ukraine said it would resume the strikes , accusing Russia of ignoring it (the Kremlin said it had never agreed to a ceasefire), and the US of withdrawing crucial support.

Zelensky has accused the US of threatening to withhold crucial intelligence if Ukraine continues striking Russian oil facilities. Trump has denied this, but last week told reporters that Zelensky had "better damn well stop" the strikes.

While in London, Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US.

Trump's deal with Russia is his administration's latest effort to lower US fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war which has seen prices skyrocket, souring his standing with the American public.
